name: IMB (Irvine-Michigan-Brookhaven)
notes: Kamiokande is recorded as a complementary experiment (the lexicographically smaller id carries the row, A1): IMB and Kamiokande both saw SN 1987A neutrinos (APS News). The APS text also says both "influence[d] the design of later detectors like Super-Kamiokande"; no source calls Super-Kamiokande a successor of IMB, so no successor row is written.
The APS releases place the mine in Painesville, Ohio; the 1987 paper says "near Fairport, Ohio". The Atlas uses the paper's wording and the Fairport Harbor village point.
The collaboration record is created because the bar asks for one where a collaboration exists (the brief did not list it); the integrator may drop it.
Proton-decay limits are recorded as the final IMB-3 analysis (Phys. Rev. D 59, 052004).

physics_goals.value: Search for proton decay in a kiloton-scale water Cherenkov detector

summary.plain: A tank of ultrapure water in an Ohio salt mine, watched by 2,048 light sensors, that began taking data in 1982 to look for the decay of protons. It found none, but on 23 February 1987 it caught eight neutrinos from supernova 1987A.
summary.technical: IMB: rectangular water Cherenkov detector with 2048 8-inch photomultipliers at 1570 m.w.e. in the Fairport Harbor Morton Salt Mine; an 8,000-ton detector, with about 5000 t active and 3300 t fiducial in the 1987 analysis; operated 1982-1991. IMB-3 set lower limits on the nucleon lifetime for many decay modes; eight neutrino events in 6 s were seen from SN 1987A.

unique_capabilities.quote: The IMB detector, the world’s first kiloton-scale nucleon decay detector, began collecting data in 1982.
